title: My Family and I
summary: A family is a fundamental unit of society whose members are related by marriage, blood or adoption and share a common roof, kitchen and source of income. A nuclear family is a couple and their children (natural or adopted) living together; a joint family has parents and siblings of the couple (three generations) living together. A family provides protection from danger to life, emotional bonding, financial and emotional security, preparation for life through education, passing of socio-cultural values, and recreation.

Beginning stage: independent young adult and marriage. Expanding stage: starts with the birth of the first child; parenting – the most challenging stage. Contracting stage: starts when the first child leaves home and ends with the last child leaving or the passing away of either partner; couples retire, pursue hobbies, take part in community service and enjoy grandchildren. Understanding the cycle helps to foresee challenges and plan priorities. Beginning stage needs: commitment, compatibility, trust, attachment; marriage should not be before 18 for a girl and 21 for a boy; preparation includes counselling on adjustment, tolerance, patience, coping with stress, financial re-planning and health security. Guidelines for healthy relationships: talk courteously, listen, be conscious of facial expressions, help each other, share responsibilities equally, look after the sick, share plans with family and express appreciation; avoid rude talk, body gestures and negative facial expressions, criticism and going out without informing. To help a new bride adjust: welcome her, accept her as part of the family, give her time and space, be realistic and non-critical.

Pregnancy: nutritious food at frequent intervals, rest and exercise, a happy atmosphere and regular check-ups; the husband and family should share work. Infancy: feeding (exclusive breast milk for 6 months), loving, clothing, bathing, immunisation; working parents may use grandparents, neighbours, day care or crèche (near home or workplace, clean, open, ventilated, qualified staff, on-call doctor, flexible timings) or a verified helper. Young children: growth depends on heredity (cannot be changed – colour of eyes, skin, height, build) and environment (managed by the parents): early stimulation, play and discipline. Infants up to two years play solitary games; children of 3–5 years play make-believe games; older children play board, computer and outdoor games that teach cooperation, sharing, team spirit and leadership; toys should be safe, inexpensive, durable, interesting and attractive, and may be low-cost and home-made.

Discipline styles: autocratic – restrictions and punishment; children lack self-confidence, are anxious, have poor communication and may become rebellious. Democratic – children are independent but under parental control, can express opinions, parents are warm and open; children are socially well adjusted, responsible and self-confident. Permissive – parents are totally uninvolved; children develop no self-control, lack social skills. School-going children (7–8 years) need little help in eating and bathing, support in studies, a separate study space, group games and good eating habits. Adolescents seek independence and identity; parents should set rules and limits, be firm yet flexible, keep communication open, trust them and give emotional support. Preparation for a career should begin early. The elderly should accept ageing, slow down and let others help; families should help them in tasks, spend time with them, meet nutritional and medical needs, involve them in decisions and respect their views.

Good family relations need understanding of duties, empathy, sensitivity, effective verbal and non-verbal communication, concern and love, help, and discretion; these are life skills. Mistrust, criticism, interference, self-centredness, lack of empathy and poor communication cause disharmony. Values (respect for elders, honesty, truthfulness, humility) are learnt in the family by direct teaching and by the parents' own example. Girls and women should not be discriminated against in nutrition, education, play, jobs or expressing opinions; equality is shown by equal nutrition, education and opportunities, recognising their contribution and respect.

objective: State True or False: (i) Eight-year-old children love to play group games. (ii) In the permissive disciplining style parents are totally involved with their children. (iii) The contracting stage of the life cycle begins when the first child leaves home. (iv) The timings of a day care should be flexible.
(i) True. (ii) False – parents are totally uninvolved. (iii) True. (iv) True.

Fill in the blanks: (i) Children brought up with the democratic disciplining style are more ______. (ii) During the ______ stage of the life cycle a couple can take part in community service and pursue hobbies. (iii) Infants up to two years are actively engaged in ______ games. (iv) When a family lives with their children under one roof it is a ______ family.
(i) socially adjusted, responsible and self-confident. (ii) contracting. (iii) solitary. (iv) nuclear.

State True or False: (i) Children of the permissive disciplining style lack social skills and self-control. (ii) Development of children is influenced by environment. (iii) Children are actively engaged in solitary games at the age of 4 to 5 years. (iv) School-going children need to develop good eating habits.
(i) True. (ii) True. (iii) False – children of 3–5 years play make-believe games; solitary play is up to 2 years. (iv) True.

Match the stage of the family life cycle with the event: (i) Beginning (ii) Expanding (iii) Contracting (iv) Retirement; (a) birth of the first child (b) marriage (c) first child leaves home (d) hobbies and grandchildren.

Match the discipline style with its result: (i) Autocratic (ii) Democratic (iii) Permissive (iv) Balanced approach for adolescents; (a) no self-control (b) self-confident, responsible (c) anxious, rebellious (d) rules with flexibility and trust.

State True or False: (i) Nuclear family has three generations. (ii) A joint family may include parents and siblings of the couple. (iii) Marriage should not happen before 18 for a girl and 21 for a boy. (iv) A new bride should be criticised so that she learns.
(i) False. (ii) True. (iii) True. (iv) False – she should be welcomed and given time and space.

Fill in the blanks: (i) Toys for children should be safe, inexpensive, durable and ______. (ii) ______ are factors that cannot be changed and are given by birth. (iii) ______ play helps children to imitate adult roles. (iv) Exclusive breast feeding should continue for ______ months.
(i) interesting and attractive. (ii) Heredity (genetic factors). (iii) Make-believe. (iv) 6.

State True or False: (i) Good relations need empathy and communication. (ii) Values are learnt only from school. (iii) Girls should have equal opportunities in nutrition and education. (iv) Elderly people should be involved in decision making.
(i) True. (ii) False – mainly from the family. (iii) True. (iv) True.
vsa: Give any four suggestions to your family to improve their relationships.

Talk to each other courteously and listen to others; share responsibilities equally; help each other and look after the sick; share plans with family members; express appreciation instead of criticising; be conscious of facial expressions and body language.
October 2025

or: What four efforts can you make to stop discrimination against your sister-in-law in your family?
Give her equal nutrition, education and opportunities; share responsibilities; recognise her contribution to the home and family income; respect her and treat her as an equal; listen to her opinions.

vsa: Briefly describe any four needs of the beginning stage of a family life cycle.

Commitment, compatibility, trust and attachment between the couple; emotional, physical, social and financial independence; adjustment with each other's families; financial re-planning and health security (contraception, pregnancy, prevention of STIs); counselling on tolerance, patience and managing stress.
April 2023
Your family has come home after a vacation. Suggest how the four family members can share household responsibilities.

Make a list of the tasks and divide them according to age and ability; rotate tasks so that no one is overloaded; each person puts things back in place; everyone shares cooking, cleaning and laundry; do the work together and appreciate each other.
April 2023
Guide your sixteen-year-old niece to act more responsibly to create peace and harmony at home.
Help with household work; talk courteously and listen; inform elders before going out; respect elders' opinions; avoid quarrelling and rude gestures; keep her room tidy and do her studies on time.
October 2022
Name the three styles of disciplining children and write one characteristic of each.

Autocratic – restrictions and punishment, children lack self-confidence. Democratic – children are independent but controlled, they are socially adjusted and self-confident. Permissive – parents are uninvolved, children lack self-control.
State four functions of a family.
Protection from danger to life; emotional bonding; financial and emotional security; preparation for life through education; passing on socio-cultural values; recreation (any four).
What is early stimulation? Give one example.

Providing ideal facilities in the early years for a child's development, e.g. talking often to the infant improves vocabulary; taking the child to a park to interact with other children speeds cognitive development.
How can the family help a newly married girl adjust in her new home?
Welcome her and accept her as an integral part; give her time and space to understand the ways of the home; have realistic expectations; be non-critical and share responsibilities.
sa: Describe the three stages of the family life cycle.

Beginning stage: the young adult becomes independent, forms intimate relationships and marries; the couple adjust to each other and both families. Expanding stage: begins with the birth of the first child; parents bear and rear children, providing for their physical, emotional, educational and social needs; the most challenging stage. Contracting stage: begins when the first child leaves home and ends with the last child leaving or the death of a partner; the couple retire, pursue hobbies, serve the community and enjoy grandchildren.
Compare the autocratic, democratic and permissive styles of disciplining children.

Autocratic: emphasis on restrictions and punishment; children lack self-confidence, are anxious and may become rebellious. Democratic: children are independent but under control; they can express opinions; parents are warm; children are socially well adjusted, responsible and confident. Permissive: parents are totally uninvolved; children develop no self-control and lack social skills.
What is the role of parents towards infants, school-going children and adolescents?

Infants: feeding, loving, clothing, bathing, immunisation and early stimulation. School-going children: support in studies, a separate study space, group games and good eating habits. Adolescents: set rules and limits, be firm and flexible, keep communication open, trust them, give emotional support and help them prepare for a career.
la: Give five suggestions by which your newly married sister can develop a good relationship with her in-laws.

(1) Talk courteously and respectfully to everyone and listen to them. (2) Share responsibilities of the house and volunteer to help. (3) Inform family members before going out or making plans. (4) Be conscious of her facial expressions and avoid negative gestures. (5) Express appreciation instead of criticising and care for the sick and elderly. (6) Neither discard nor impose her beliefs but create a better, practical option; give time to adjust.
Explain why the family is important and how it passes on values and helps to build life skills.

The family provides protection, emotional bonding, financial and emotional security, education and recreation. Parents teach values (respect for elders, honesty, humility) by telling children what to do and by setting examples. Good relations need life skills such as empathy, communication, concern, help and discretion, and the family must show equality towards girls and women and care for the elderly and sick, giving every member unconditional love, care and support.
